entry.label: 32 Key Concepts in Systems Thinking and Complexity Theory
entry.description: A 2024 unFIX visual and explanatory synthesis which places 32 systems-thinking and complexity concepts on a relative continuum. Its author states that AI systems produced the initial synthesis and prevalence estimates, followed by editorial checking.
entry.canonical_definition: A 2024 unFIX visual and explanatory synthesis which places 32 systems-thinking and complexity concepts on a relative continuum. Its author states that AI systems produced the initial synthesis and prevalence estimates, followed by editorial checking.

profile.summary: The unFIX 32-concept synthesis is a public comparator: it offers a broad route into familiar systems and complexity terms while making its AI-assisted production method explicit.
profile.canonical_definition: The unFIX 32-concept synthesis is a public comparator: it offers a broad route into familiar systems and complexity terms while making its AI-assisted production method explicit.
profile.why_it_matters: It is useful for testing atlas coverage and search language. It is not evidence that the selected concepts, definitions or prevalence scores form a settled canon.
key_distinctions: Inclusion in the list is documentary evidence about the unFIX synthesis, not independent evidence of intellectual importance.
The systems-thinking/complexity scores are editorial and AI-assisted estimates, not measurements of a defined literature corpus.
dependent_subsequents: comparison with a typed evidence graph
common_misreadings: A colourful map is not automatically a genealogy, taxonomy or source-backed relation graph.
open_checks: Retain disagreement about labels and placement; do not copy the list's boundary as the atlas boundary.

entry.label: Adaptation
entry.description: Adaptation is relational: change is adaptive only with respect to some environment, timescale and viability condition. Local adjustment can make the larger system more fragile.
entry.canonical_definition: Change in a system's organisation, behaviour or relations that improves or preserves its capacity to remain viable in a changing environment.

profile.title: Adaptation
profile.canonical_definition: Change in a system's organisation, behaviour or relations that improves or preserves its capacity to remain viable in a changing environment.
profile.summary: Adaptation is relational: change is adaptive only with respect to some environment, timescale and viability condition. Local adjustment can make the larger system more fragile.
profile.why_it_matters: Transformation programmes often demand change without specifying what environmental variety has changed or what identity must be preserved. The result is motion rather than adaptation.
practice_connections: state what changed in the environment
retain variety and slack for unknown change
common_misreadings: adaptation is always improvement
survival proves good design
optimisation increases adaptability
change at one level helps every level
open_checks: Ashby and ultrastability
Beer System 4
evolutionary adaptation
path dependence and maladaptation

profile.title: Anthro-complexity
profile.canonical_definition: A body of theory and practice concerned with complexity in human systems, foregrounding meaning, intentionality, identity, narrative and the limits of treating people as interchangeable agents.
profile.summary: Anthro-complexity addresses complexity in human systems without treating people as simple agents analogous to insects, particles or interchangeable units. It foregrounds meaning, play, making, narrative, identity and intentionality.
profile.why_it_matters: Human beings can act on descriptions, change identity, contest purposes and alter the rules. These capacities affect what can be carried across from computational or biological complexity models.

natural science constraint vs direct social analogy

computational complexity is rejected rather than bounded
anthro-complexity is the only account of social complexity

entry.description: A network produces components that regenerate that network and constitute it as a distinguishable unity. The 1974 paper makes this a specific organisational condition, not a synonym for persistence.

profile.title: Autopoiesis
profile.summary: The biological account includes the production of a boundary that enables the processes producing it. Material turnover is compatible with the persistence of this organisation.
profile.canonical_definition: Self-production of a unity through a recursively constituted network of component production.
profile.why_it_matters: A boundary drawn by an analyst and a boundary produced by a living system make different claims.
practice_connections: Before applying the term, identify components, production processes, and boundary formation.
common_misreadings: Any durable feedback loop is autopoietic.

profile.title: Benjamin P Taylor
profile.canonical_definition: Systems practitioner, educator, and writer working on public-service transformation, organisational capability, and the use of systems and cybernetic ideas in practice. He leads RedQuadrant and the Public Service Transformation Academy, serves on the SCiO board, and curates the Systems Community of Inquiry and The Necessary Tangle.
profile.summary: Taylor’s public work moves between work with services and organisations, practitioner education, writing, and community curation. His teaching includes the Viable System Model (VSM), large-group processes, constructive conversations, and distinctions between systems leadership, systems change, systems practice, and systems convening. His current papers with Philip Boxer examine relational public services, demand, organisational boundaries, and the conditions under which learning can change an institution’s response.
profile.why_it_matters: The contribution represented here is the work of translating, combining, testing, and teaching ideas in public-service and organisational settings. Examples include the four dynamics of organisation, five core leadership practices, and the degrees-of-relationality heuristic. These should be read as specific, attributable practice accounts with their own sources and limits. The public archive also offers a route from a problem in practice to a teaching account, an underlying concept, and competing ways of framing it.
key_distinctions: Systems leadership, systems change, systems practice, and systems convening do different work, even where they overlap.
A reliable transaction can be appropriate; relationality is not automatically an improvement.
Teaching, adaptation, authorship, and curation are different contributions.
An organisation’s service categories do not exhaust what matters in a citizen’s life.
historical_lineage: Four dynamics: the 2024 ISSS presentation explicitly names Barry Oshry, Stafford Beer, and Sandra Janoff as sources for the synthesis.
Management cybernetics and the Viable System Model appear in named public lectures and practical adaptations.
Co-authored working papers with Philip Boxer address asymmetric demand and relational public-service reform.
logical_antecedents: Learning, constructive conversation, and public purpose
dependent_subsequents: Degrees of relationality: a ladder for public service design
The Necessary Tangle and the public work library
practice_connections: Public-service transformation and capability development through RedQuadrant and PSTA
SCiO professional practice, events, and education
Systems convening and work across organisational boundaries
Public writing at Chosen Path and curation through SysCoI
espoused_lineages: Oshry, Beer, and Janoff are explicitly named in the four-dynamics presentation; this is not a general claim of personal mentorship.
common_misreadings: Hosting or curating a work does not make Taylor its author.
The degrees-of-relationality ladder is a heuristic, not a moral ranking or validated maturity scale.
Presenting the VSM does not imply originating it.
open_checks: Add independent accounts of practice and outcomes, distinguishing testimony from evaluated evidence.
Continue reconciling older writing and training records, including editions and co-author credits.
Develop further passage-level connections from the four requested research collections.

entry.label: Boundary
entry.description: A boundary makes inquiry and action possible by limiting what must be handled at once. It also externalises people, effects and responsibilities. Good systems work therefore treats boundary choice as practical, political and ethical.
entry.canonical_definition: A purpose- and observer-dependent distinction that marks what is treated as inside, outside or marginal to a system of concern and thereby shapes explanation, legitimacy and intervention.

profile.title: Boundary critique
profile.canonical_definition: Boundary critique is the systematic examination of judgements about what and whom a situation, inquiry or proposal treats as relevant, including the facts, values, interests and voices those judgements admit or exclude.
profile.summary: Boundary critique asks how judgements about relevance shape what counts as fact, value, improvement, expertise and legitimate participation.
profile.why_it_matters: Every systems intervention draws a boundary. Making that boundary discussable is a condition for responsible inquiry, especially when benefits and harms fall on people who did not define the system of concern.

all boundaries can be eliminated
boundary critique guarantees inclusion

profile.title: Bounded applicability
profile.canonical_definition: Principle that approaches have conditions under which they are useful and should not be treated as context-free universal solutions.
profile.summary: Bounded applicability says that a method or explanation earns validity within specified conditions rather than by being asserted as a context-free solution.
profile.why_it_matters: It is a useful antidote to method fundamentalism. It also imposes work: the boundary, evidence and transition conditions must be made explicit rather than invoked as a general escape clause.

entry.label: Chris Mowles
entry.description: A scholar and practitioner of complexity and management whose work argues for a radically social account of organisational continuity and change, with attention to interaction, power, uncertainty and practical judgement.

profile.summary: Chris Mowles develops a critical and practice-facing account of complexity in social and organisational life. His work presses against the idea that complexity thinking supplies managers with a better control technology.
profile.why_it_matters: The atlas is much stronger on formal and cybernetic concepts than on the difficulty of moving from models of natural complex systems to accounts of human interaction. Mowles provides a documented challenge to that transfer and a route into power, politics, improvisation and practical judgement.
key_distinctions: Complexity as a description of social life is not the same as complexity science used as a managerial toolkit.
Unpredictability does not remove responsibility or practical judgement.
Organisations are ongoing patterns of interaction, not containers standing apart from the people who constitute them.
historical_lineage: The work continues the University of Hertfordshire community of inquiry associated with Ralph Stacey and complex responsive processes.
It draws critically on complexity sciences while also using pragmatic, sociological, psychodynamic and organisational traditions.
common_misreadings: That accepting unpredictability means giving up on deliberate action.
That complex responsive processes is simply another systems model of an organisation.
That a critique of control is a claim that power disappears.
open_checks: Develop the wider Hertfordshire community constellation and document disagreement within and around it.
Compare Mowles's use of complexity with systems-practice, critical-systems and complexity-leadership traditions.

entry.label: Complex responsive processes
entry.description: A perspective on organising in which continuity, novelty, identity and power emerge in local interaction among interdependent people rather than being the straightforward implementation of a system-wide plan.

profile.summary: Complex responsive processes treats organising as the ongoing patterning of local interaction. Broader organisational patterns constrain and enable action, but they do not operate as an external system that a manager can stand outside and control.
profile.why_it_matters: It exposes a fault line inside systems | cybernetics | complexity: whether models of systems and self-organisation illuminate human organising or quietly reintroduce an engineer standing outside the situation.
key_distinctions: Local interaction and population-wide pattern are mutually constitutive.
Power is present in ordinary interaction rather than added later as a contextual variable.
Emergence does not imply harmony, decentralisation or benign self-organisation.
historical_lineage: Developed in the University of Hertfordshire Complexity and Management community, especially through Ralph Stacey and colleagues.
Uses complexity sciences as resources for analogy while explicitly disputing some systems metaphors for human action.
practice_connections: Attending to live interaction rather than treating plans as causes of later outcomes.
Developing practical judgement through reflexive inquiry.
Taking conflict, identity and power seriously in accounts of organisational change.
common_misreadings: That local interaction means small-scale interaction is all that matters.
That no one controls the whole means no one has more power than anyone else.
That emergence explains an outcome without a detailed account of interaction and history.
open_checks: Represent its critiques of systems thinking without caricaturing the many systems traditions it addresses.
Trace its relationship to pragmatism, group analysis, Elias, Mead and Hegel using primary and scholarly sources.

Models can sharpen judgement without determining action.
Predictable unpredictability is not a licence for vague claims about anything being complex.

entry.label: Conant-Ashby Theorem
entry.description: The Conant–Ashby theorem states, under the assumptions of the original formal paper, that the simplest optimal regulator must embody a model of what it regulates. Popular uses should not erase those assumptions or turn every useful representation into a proof of optimal control.
entry.canonical_definition: Under the paper's assumptions, a simplest optimal regulator is representable by a mapping h: S → R.

profile.title: Conant-Ashby Theorem
profile.summary: The result concerns the simplest regulator among those minimising outcome entropy. Its model is a mapping from reguland events to regulatory actions.
profile.canonical_definition: Under the paper's assumptions, a simplest optimal regulator is representable by a mapping h: S → R.
profile.why_it_matters: A diagram or forecast is not sufficient evidence that an organisation regulates successfully.
key_distinctions: an embodied mapping versus an explicit representation
a theorem's assumptions versus an organisational analogy
practice_connections: State which outcomes count as successful before invoking optimality.
common_misreadings: Every regulator is optimal.
The model must be a conscious simulation.
open_checks: Assess how the theorem's fixed distribution and outcome criterion fit the proposed application.

profile.title: Cynefin framework
profile.canonical_definition: Decision-support framework for discerning context and choosing approaches on the basis of bounded applicability, distinguishing ordered, complex, chaotic and aporetic conditions and their dynamics.
profile.summary: Cynefin is a context-discrimination and decision-support framework. It asks which causal conditions and constraints are present, which approaches are applicable, and when a shift in context requires a change of method.
profile.why_it_matters: It counters the habit of treating one method as universally valid. Its domains are most useful when treated dynamically and provisionally rather than as labels attached permanently to problems.
key_distinctions: clear and complicated order vs complexity vs chaos
historical_lineage: A Leader's Framework for Decision Making

complex is a synonym for difficult
the quadrants are maturity levels
anything uncertain belongs in complexity
the framework itself supplies a complete intervention

represent liminal domains and aporia
add empirical applications and criticism

profile.title: Damian Allen
profile.canonical_definition: Chief Executive of City of Doncaster Council and a systems practitioner whose stated lineage joins ecology, philosophy, learning, systems, complexity, cybernetics, design, place, regeneration and relational public services.

entry.description: Double-loop learning changes not only an action but the governing assumptions, values or rules by which the action was chosen. It is distinguished from correcting performance while leaving those rules intact.

entry.label: Emergence
entry.description: The appearance at one scale of properties, patterns or capacities not straightforwardly present at another scale, arising through interactions and organisation. It describes a relation across levels; it is not a hidden causal substance.
entry.canonical_definition: A relation across levels or scales in which a macro-property or pattern arises from interactions among lower-level components yet is not usefully reducible to a simple inventory of those components.

profile.title: Emergence
profile.canonical_definition: A relation across levels or scales in which a macro-property or pattern arises from interactions among lower-level components yet is not usefully reducible to a simple inventory of those components.
profile.summary: Emergence names a relation across levels: interactions among parts produce a pattern, property or capacity visible at another scale. It can mark genuine explanatory work, but the word becomes empty when used instead of specifying mechanisms and conditions.
profile.why_it_matters: Complex outcomes cannot usually be attributed to one actor or intervention. Emergence helps resist linear claims of delivery and control. It does not mean outcomes are uncaused, magical or beyond all inquiry.
key_distinctions: weak or epistemic emergence vs stronger ontological claims
novel pattern vs surprise to an observer
practice_connections: stop claiming to deliver outcomes produced by many interacting agents
look for conditions and feedback rather than single causes
state the scale at which the property appears
use experiments and probes without pretending they command the whole
common_misreadings: emergence is a force
emergent means unpredictable
calling something emergent explains it
emergence guarantees novelty or improvement
open_checks: Lewes and historical terminology
strong vs weak emergence
causal emergence
public-service outcome applications

profile.title: Feedback
profile.canonical_definition: A circular causal or informational relation in which an output or consequence affects later input, state or action. The sign, delay, reference condition and mechanism must be stated.
profile.summary: Feedback is not merely receiving comments. It is a circular relation in which consequences return to influence what happens next. The loop may counteract change, reinforce it, oscillate, delay response or fail because no actor can use the returned information.
profile.why_it_matters: Systems work often says feedback when it means reporting, evaluation, data or learning. Those are only feedback when they close a loop that can alter subsequent action. Sign, delay, reference condition and response capacity determine what the loop actually does.
key_distinctions: negative or balancing vs positive or reinforcing feedback
feedback signal vs capacity to respond
physical causal loop vs returned information
historical_lineage: Maxwell 1868: mathematical governor analysis as a precursor
Rosenblueth, Wiener and Bigelow 1943: purposive behaviour and negative feedback
Wiener 1948: cybernetic synthesis across animals and machines
logical_antecedents: a return path through which consequences can alter later conditions
a reference or viability condition where correction is claimed
practice_connections: ask what information returns to whom
test whether anyone can alter action in response
state the delay before effects become visible
look for loops that reward gaming rather than purpose
common_misreadings: more feedback is always better
positive means good and negative means bad
a dashboard is feedback even when nobody can act
homeostasis and feedback are synonyms
all loops stabilise
open_checks: Nyquist and Bode lineage
Forrester and system dynamics
Bateson, Argyris and learning
Beer and organisational feedback channels

claims.statement: Maxwell's 'On Governors' is a historical precursor to later mathematical feedback and control analysis; this does not imply that Maxwell used the later cybernetic concept or terminology.

claims.statement: Positive and negative feedback name the sign and effect of a loop, not whether the result is morally or practically good or bad.
claims.notes: Core orientation claim for non-specialist readers.

claims.statement: Feedback is a definitional prerequisite for Wiener's 1948 formulation of cybernetics, while later cybernetics may frame the field more broadly.

sources.title: Systems Thinking Practitioner apprenticeship standard ST0787 v1.2
sources.notes: Current approved standard; requires concepts, laws, provenance, schools, ontology, epistemology, approaches, intervention, ethics and evaluation.

sources.title: On Governors
sources.notes: James Clerk Maxwell, Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, vol. 16, pp. 270–283. Bibliographic records span 1867–1868. Used here as a historical precursor to mathematical analysis of governors and control; it does not use the later cybernetic vocabulary of feedback.

sources.title: Stabilized Feedback Amplifiers
sources.notes: H. S. Black, Bell System Technical Journal 13(1), pp. 1–18. Primary engineering account of the negative-feedback amplifier principle. The invention predates the paper; this release does not make a first-invention claim.

sources.title: Behavior, Purpose and Teleology
sources.notes: Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow, Philosophy of Science 10(1), pp. 18–24. Primary pre-cybernetics article connecting purposive behaviour with input/output relations and negative feedback.

sources.title: Cybernetics or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine
sources.notes: Norbert Wiener's foundational synthesis, first published in 1948. The MIT Press open-access reissue describes feedback and information as central to the field. Exact chapter-level use remains a next editorial check.
sources.licence: CC BY-NC-ND for the open-access reissue

sources.title: Organization for Physiological Homeostasis
sources.notes: Walter B. Cannon, Physiological Reviews 9(3), pp. 399-431. Primary article establishing the physiological homeostasis formulation. This release uses bibliographic and article-level evidence and does not reduce homeostasis to feedback.

sources.title: Feedback - IEEE Technology Navigator
sources.notes: Technical overview distinguishing negative and positive feedback and describing their different effects. Used as an orientation source, not as the sole historical authority.

sources.notes: Lists 33 systems laws and principles and describes nine patterns of thinking.

sources.title: The Grammar of Systems II: From Order to Chaos and Back Again, 2nd edition

sources.title: 32 Key Concepts in Systems Thinking and Complexity Theory

sources.title: Study of System Dynamics

entry.label: Feedforward
entry.description: Anticipatory action based on a desired future, a measured disturbance or a model of likely effects, taken before the resulting output is available for correction.
entry.canonical_definition: A control or coordination relation in which information about intended conditions or measured disturbances is used to act before the resulting output is observed; effectiveness depends on the adequacy of the model or prediction.

profile.title: Feedforward
profile.canonical_definition: A control or coordination relation in which information about intended conditions or measured disturbances is used to act before the resulting output is observed; effectiveness depends on the adequacy of the model or prediction.
profile.summary: Feedforward acts before the result is available to be measured. It uses intention, forecast or measured disturbance to shape action in advance. It is usually strongest when combined with feedback that corrects modelling error and surprise.
profile.why_it_matters: Waiting for failure before responding is often costly. Feedforward can prepare capacity, prevent deviation and make intentions interpretable. Its weakness is that it depends on the quality of the model, forecast and disturbance sensing.
key_distinctions: anticipatory action vs reaction to output
historical_lineage: anticipatory control developed alongside feedback control
the term also developed a communication meaning in cybernetic discussions
modern engineering commonly combines feedforward with feedback
logical_antecedents: a model or expectation of effects
capacity to act before output changes
practice_connections: ask what can be known early enough to matter
state the assumptions in the predictive model
common_misreadings: feedback supplied early
perfect prediction
a substitute for feedback
any plan is feedforward
open_checks: I. A. Richards and Macy lineage
management-cybernetics uses
predictive control literature

entry.label: Homeostasis
entry.description: Dynamic maintenance or restoration of internal variables within viable ranges despite disturbance. It is neither immobility nor a synonym for a single feedback loop.
entry.canonical_definition: The organised maintenance of internal variables within viable ranges despite disturbance; the relevant variables, ranges, mechanisms and time scales must be specified.

profile.title: Homeostasis
profile.canonical_definition: The organised maintenance of internal variables within viable ranges despite disturbance; the relevant variables, ranges, mechanisms and time scales must be specified.
profile.summary: Homeostasis is dynamic maintenance, not stillness. A living system keeps selected internal variables within viable ranges while energy, matter and information continue to flow and conditions continue to change.
profile.why_it_matters: The idea is useful for understanding stability and resistance to disturbance. In organisations it is often used metaphorically; the metaphor only earns its keep when the variables, ranges and mechanisms being maintained are named.
key_distinctions: maintained condition vs one feedback loop
viable range vs exact set point
historical_lineage: Claude Bernard: internal milieu as precursor
cybernetics connected homeostasis with regulation and feedback
practice_connections: ask what the system is working to keep unchanged
look for hidden work that maintains dysfunction
identify who benefits from the maintained state
common_misreadings: nothing changes
homeostasis is always desirable
all resistance is irrational
feedback and homeostasis are synonyms
open_checks: Bernard primary lineage
allostasis and adaptive ranges
responsible use in social systems
profile.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.

entry.label: Information
entry.description: Information is not raw stuff that flows unchanged through channels. A signal becomes information only within some receiving organisation, code, concern or capacity to respond.
entry.canonical_definition: A difference selected and taken up within an organised context so that it can alter expectation, state or action; its mathematical measure is distinct from meaning and use.

profile.title: Information
profile.canonical_definition: A difference selected and taken up within an organised context so that it can alter expectation, state or action; its mathematical measure is distinct from meaning and use.
profile.summary: Information is not raw stuff that flows unchanged through channels. A signal becomes information only within some receiving organisation, code, concern or capacity to respond. Bateson's formulation selects differences through their effects within a circuit. It does not turn the mathematical quantity of information into a measure of meaning.
profile.why_it_matters: Public and organisational systems routinely confuse data volume with understanding. The key questions are what differences are sensed, how they are coded, who can interpret them and what action they enable. Ask what changed for the recipient, not merely what was transmitted.
key_distinctions: difference available versus difference taken up
practice_connections: check whether the receiver has a code and response repertoire
reduce reporting that cannot affect action
Trace a report through the action it enables, blocks, or fails to change.
common_misreadings: information is meaning
more data means more information
signals cross boundaries unchanged
information automatically produces learning
Sending a message proves it informed someone.
open_checks: Bateson's formulations
semantic information
algorithmic information
information and affordance
Keep the several meanings of information explicit.

entry.label: Information theory
entry.description: A mathematical theory of communication and uncertainty. Shannon information concerns the selection and transmission of possibilities under probability and noise; it does not by itself supply semantic meaning or value.
entry.canonical_definition: The mathematical study of the quantification, coding and reliable transmission of uncertainty-bearing signals, including entropy, channel capacity, redundancy and noise.

profile.title: Information theory
profile.canonical_definition: The mathematical study of the quantification, coding and reliable transmission of uncertainty-bearing signals, including entropy, channel capacity, redundancy and noise.
profile.summary: Information theory supplies a mathematical account of uncertainty, coding and communication through noisy channels. It is powerful precisely because it brackets semantic meaning and studies the structure and limits of transmission.
profile.why_it_matters: Systems and cybernetics use information in several senses. Confusing Shannon information with meaning, truth, knowledge or value produces category errors. The mathematical theory can tell us how much uncertainty is reduced, not whether the message is wise, accurate or humane.
key_distinctions: entropy vs disorder as a loose metaphor
historical_lineage: Nyquist and Hartley as technical precursors
Wiener 1948: cybernetic use of information and control
Ashby: information and variety in regulation
logical_antecedents: a set of possible messages or states
practice_connections: ask what uncertainty is reduced for which decision
measure the channel as well as the message
notice what the classification scheme makes invisible
common_misreadings: information means meaning
more data means better knowledge
entropy is simply chaos
a message has the same informational value to every observer
open_checks: Hartley and Nyquist lineage
Ashby-Shannon formal relation
semantic information traditions

entry.description: A returned effect that counteracts deviation or change. It often supports regulation and stability, but excessive gain or delay can also create oscillation or instability.

profile.title: Negative feedback
profile.canonical_definition: A feedback relation in which the returned effect opposes a change or deviation in the relevant variable; the reference condition, loop gain, delay and mechanism must be specified.
profile.summary: Negative feedback returns an effect that opposes deviation or change. It is the basis of many stabilising mechanisms, but its result depends on gain, delay, measurement and the dynamics of the system being regulated.
profile.why_it_matters: The phrase is often used as if negative means criticism or undesirable effects. In technical use it describes loop sign. Poorly timed or overpowered negative feedback can oscillate or destabilise rather than calmly restore a set point.
key_distinctions: explicit set point vs implicit viable range
error correction vs suppression of useful variation
historical_lineage: Rosenblueth, Wiener and Bigelow 1943: goal-directed behaviour and negative feedback
logical_antecedents: deviation or change to be opposed
practice_connections: check whether the correction arrives too late
ask what useful variation is being damped
avoid assuming tighter control is better control
identify who sets the reference condition
common_misreadings: negative feedback is criticism
it always produces stability
it requires a humanly stated target
it is always ethically desirable
open_checks: Bode and Nyquist stability analysis
physiological mechanisms beyond simple loops
profile.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.

entry.label: Organisational recursion
entry.description: A domain-specific use of recursion in which operational units may themselves be treated as viable systems with corresponding requirements at another level. Visual nesting alone is not enough.

profile.title: Organisational recursion
profile.canonical_definition: A domain-specific use of recursion in which an organisational system contains operational units that may themselves be treated as systems with structurally corresponding viability requirements at another level.
profile.summary: In the VSM tradition, a viable operational unit may itself contain operations and meta-systemic functions. The same broad viability requirements recur, while purpose, environment, scale and implementation differ at each level.
profile.why_it_matters: Organisations often centralise decisions that require local variety or mistake reporting lines for system levels. Recursion helps locate the system-in-focus and test whether each operational unit has sufficient autonomy and regulatory support.
key_distinctions: recursive viability vs repeated organisation chart
historical_lineage: Stafford Beer developed recursive viability within management cybernetics
Diagnosing the System for Organizations made the model operational
later VSM practice developed recursive mapping techniques
practice_connections: test whether operational units are genuinely viable or merely departments
avoid forcing one diagram onto every scale
common_misreadings: every hierarchy is recursive
recursion means the same five departments at every level
autonomy means no coordination
one VSM diagram represents the whole organisation once and for all
open_checks: exact Beer primary passages
comparative practice evidence
limits and critiques of recursive mapping
profile.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.

profile.title: Positive feedback
profile.canonical_definition: A feedback relation in which the returned effect reinforces rather than counteracts a change in the relevant variable; the sign, loop gain, delay and limiting conditions must be specified.
profile.summary: Positive feedback reinforces change. It can create growth, escalation, tipping, latching, path dependence or oscillation. What stops the process is usually found in constraints, saturation, resource limits or another balancing loop.
profile.why_it_matters: Reinforcing loops explain why small differences can become large and why systems can move rapidly away from an apparently stable condition. They are central to contagion, polarisation, bubbles, collapse, learning and mobilisation, but are not inherently beneficial or harmful.
key_distinctions: reinforcing loop vs exponential growth without limit
historical_lineage: early regenerative circuits predate the cybernetic synthesis
mid-century control and cybernetics established positive and negative loop language
system dynamics popularised reinforcing loop notation
logical_antecedents: returned effect aligned with the direction of change
dependent_subsequents: escalation and vicious or virtuous circles
practice_connections: look for the limit that eventually stops growth
do not label the loop virtuous or vicious before examining consequences
test whether intervention also strengthens the loop
common_misreadings: positive means good
reinforcing growth continues forever
all positive feedback is instability
praise is the technical meaning
open_checks: historical lineage before Black
system dynamics source locators
nonlinear and tipping-point literature

entry.label: Recursion
entry.description: A family of relations in which a definition, operation, organisation or observation is reapplied to instances of the same kind. The domain, recurrence rule and boundary condition must be stated.
entry.canonical_definition: A family of domain-specific relations in which a definition, operation, structure or organisation is reapplied to instances of the same kind. A conforming account must state the domain, recurrence rule and boundary or termination condition; organisational recursion is not automatically computational recursion or visual self-similarity.

profile.title: Recursion
profile.canonical_definition: A family of domain-specific relations in which a definition, operation, structure or organisation is reapplied to instances of the same kind. A conforming account must state the domain, recurrence rule and boundary or termination condition; organisational recursion is not automatically computational recursion or visual self-similarity.
profile.summary: Recursion is a family resemblance across domains, not one universal mechanism. A definition may refer to itself through smaller cases; a computation may call itself; an organisation may contain operational systems with corresponding viability requirements.
profile.why_it_matters: Nested diagrams easily look profound. A sound recursive claim states what recurs, what changes between levels, what the base or boundary condition is and why the same structural relation applies.
historical_lineage: formal recursive definition and recursive-function theory
second-order observation and reflexivity as a distinct neighbouring lineage
logical_antecedents: identity of the operation or structure
rule for moving to another instance or level
domain in which sameness is claimed
practice_connections: show what recurs and what does not
do not infer sameness from visual nesting
common_misreadings: repetition is recursion
hierarchy and recursion are synonyms
fractal means recursive and vice versa
Turing invented recursion
nested boxes prove organisational recursion

entry.description: The constraint of possible outcomes under disturbance in relation to specified goals, essential variables or acceptable states. Regulation can use feedback, feedforward, structure, constraint or combinations of them.

profile.title: Regulation
profile.canonical_definition: A relation among disturbances, a reguland, a regulator and acceptable outcomes in which outcome variety is constrained relative to a stated goal or essential-variable range.
profile.summary: Regulation is the work of keeping outcomes within acceptable ranges despite disturbance. It may operate through feedback, anticipation, constraints, buffering, redundancy, local autonomy or changes to the environment.
profile.why_it_matters: Regulation is often collapsed into command and control. Ashby instead asks what variety of disturbance reaches the system, what responses are available and which outcomes count as acceptable. The regulator may be distributed rather than a boss or central unit.
key_distinctions: acceptable range vs one fixed target
historical_lineage: physiological regulation and governor analysis predate cybernetics
Ashby formalised regulation in terms of variety and outcomes
practice_connections: identify the variable that must remain viable
map disturbance variety before adding controls
ask where regulatory intelligence already sits
protect local discretion where it carries necessary variety
common_misreadings: regulation means bureaucracy
the regulator must be central
tighter control always improves regulation
one target captures viability
open_checks: legal and institutional regulation as a distinct lineage
distributed regulation cases

entry.label: Requisite variety
entry.description: The regulatory requirement and limit expressed by Ashby: reducing outcome variety depends on the regulator having usable discriminations and responses relative to disturbances and constraints.
entry.canonical_definition: The variety needed in a regulator, given disturbances, transformations and acceptable outcomes, to achieve the intended reduction in outcome variety. It is a limit on regulation, not a general instruction to maximise complication.

profile.title: Requisite variety
profile.canonical_definition: The variety needed in a regulator, given disturbances, transformations and acceptable outcomes, to achieve the intended reduction in outcome variety. It is a limit on regulation, not a general instruction to maximise complication.
profile.summary: Ashby's law sets a limit on regulation. Disturbance variety can only be reduced to the extent that the regulator has relevant, selectable and effective response variety within the transformation being regulated. Ashby's bound depends on the disturbance–response table. Section 11/9 also allows the transformation itself to remove variety.
profile.why_it_matters: The slogan is often used to justify more choice, more management or decentralisation in the abstract. The law asks a harder question: which responses can distinguish and counter which disturbances, under what communication and resource constraints? Count responses that can actually be selected and act, rather than nominal options.
key_distinctions: attenuation and amplification vs maximal complication
law of requisite variety vs good regulator theorem
necessary regulatory capacity vs a universal organisational prescription
raw disturbance variety versus variety reaching the regulated outcome
historical_lineage: Conant and Ashby 1970: good regulator theorem
Beer: application in management cybernetics and VSM
practice_connections: map where variety is generated, attenuated and amplified
increase response repertoire only where it can affect outcomes
reduce avoidable disturbance rather than merely adding control
protect local autonomy where it carries relevant knowledge
Specify disturbances, responses, and acceptable outcomes before applying the inequality.
common_misreadings: the controller must simply be more complicated
more choice is always better
the theorem proves decentralisation in every case
the good regulator theorem is the same theorem
The regulator must reproduce every environmental detail.
open_checks: exact provenance of absorb variety wording
Beer primary application pages
empirical organisational applications
Test any organisational mapping against the formal assumptions.

profile.canonical_definition: Robert Rosen was a theoretical biologist whose work addressed relational biology, anticipatory systems, modelling, and the organisation of living systems. His scientific-work archive provides routes into the corpus; Springer identifies him as the author of Anticipatory Systems, and ISSS records his presidency in 1980–81.
profile.why_it_matters: Rosen matters to systems inquiry because he treated modelling and anticipation as constitutive questions for living organisation, not merely as techniques for forecasting it.
key_distinctions: Anticipation is not the same as prediction.
A modelling relation is not interchangeable with a computer simulation.
An archive landing page locates a corpus; it does not settle interpretations of Rosen's mathematics.
historical_lineage: Relational biology, mathematical biology, and anticipatory systems.
practice_connections: Distinguish a model used by an anticipatory organisation from an observer's external simulation of that organisation.

entry.label: Self-organisation
entry.description: The development of global order or coordination through local interactions without an external central controller specifying the resulting pattern. Boundaries, constraints, energy and environment still matter.
entry.canonical_definition: A process in which interactions among components generate or maintain an organised macro-pattern without a central external controller prescribing that pattern; the system boundary, local rules, constraints and environment must be specified.

profile.title: Self-organisation
profile.canonical_definition: A process in which interactions among components generate or maintain an organised macro-pattern without a central external controller prescribing that pattern; the system boundary, local rules, constraints and environment must be specified.
profile.summary: Self-organisation describes organised macro-patterns arising through interactions among components rather than being prescribed by an external central controller. The system still depends on boundaries, local rules, resources, constraints and an environment.
profile.why_it_matters: The phrase is often instrumentalised as if leaders can order emergence or simply withdraw. A useful account specifies the local interactions, constraints and selection processes that generate the pattern, and asks who drew the system boundary.
key_distinctions: no central prescription vs no causes or constraints
description by an observer vs intrinsic organisation
historical_lineage: von Foerster 1960: systems and environments, order from noise
later complexity science: local interaction and global pattern
practice_connections: specify what interactions are being enabled or blocked
look for power embedded in rules and resources
do not treat leaderless as ungoverned
intervene in conditions rather than promise a designed outcome
common_misreadings: no management is required
the system organises itself towards good ends
emergence and self-organisation are synonyms
constraints prevent self-organisation
open_checks: Prigogine and dissipative structures
autopoiesis
agent-based modelling lineage

entry.label: Structural coupling
entry.description: Repeated system-environment interaction can shape the structures through which further interaction occurs. The FEM project uses this idea to identify consequential enterprise-environment relationships; that application is narrower than the biological concept.
entry.canonical_definition: Repeated interactions through which systems and their environments shape the structures governing later interactions. In Maturana's biological account, these structural changes conserve the system's defining organisation.

profile.title: Structural coupling
profile.summary: Maturana distinguishes a perturbation that triggers change from an instruction that specifies it: the current structure determines the response. Fractal Enterprise Model practice uses structural coupling to examine consequential enterprise–environment relationships; that application requires its own account of the participating systems and interactions.
profile.canonical_definition: Repeated interactions through which systems and their environments shape the structures governing later interactions. In Maturana's biological account, these structural changes conserve the system's defining organisation.
profile.why_it_matters: A repeated message can meet a changing recipient. Communication problems may involve the history of the relationship as well as the message.
practice_connections: Trace how repeated interactions alter the parties' capacity to respond; treat this as an interpretive question, not a biological diagnosis.
common_misreadings: Coupling implies agreement.
An external message determines the recipient's response.
open_checks: Evidence is needed for any proposed organisational application.

entry.label: Systemic Intervention
entry.description: Systemic Intervention combines critical reflection on boundaries with methodological pluralism and action. It treats intervention choices as practical, political and ethical rather than technically neutral.
entry.canonical_definition: A systemic methodology that begins with critical reflection on boundaries and values, then draws on methodological pluralism to support responsible action in complex situations.

profile.title: Systemic Intervention
profile.canonical_definition: A systemic methodology that begins with critical reflection on boundaries and values, then draws on methodological pluralism to support responsible action in complex situations.
profile.summary: Systemic Intervention refuses the idea that the problem and method are already given. It asks how boundaries and values create marginalisation, then selects and combines methods in relation to the situation.
profile.why_it_matters: Method choice is itself an intervention. Boundary critique helps practitioners see whose concerns, knowledge and consequences are being made central or peripheral.

entry.label: Systems change
entry.description: An overloaded family of practices concerned with altering patterns, structures, relations, purposes or conditions across a system of concern. Systems are already changing, so the phrase needs a boundary, direction, account of agency, legitimacy and theory of change.

profile.title: Systems change
profile.canonical_definition: An overloaded family of practices concerned with altering patterns, structures, relations, purposes or conditions across a system of concern. Systems are already changing, so the phrase needs a boundary, direction, account of agency, legitimacy and theory of change.
profile.summary: Systems change is a family name for efforts to alter enduring patterns, relations, structures, purposes or conditions across a system of concern. The system, the desired direction and the authority to judge improvement must be stated rather than smuggled in.
profile.why_it_matters: The phrase can reify 'the system' as a concrete object waiting to be redesigned. It can also hide the fact that systems are always changing and that deliberate intervention is only one source of change.
key_distinctions: change in a system vs changing a system of concern
system improvement vs changes in legitimacy or purpose
planned intervention vs emergence and cultural evolution
integration of fragmentation vs replacement with a new order
historical_lineage: complexity-informed accounts of emergence and adaptation
practice_connections: name the current and desired patterns without pretending either is complete
identify who can act and who bears the effects
treat interventions as probes which generate learning
common_misreadings: that a system is static before a programme changes it
that a map identifies a controllable whole
that beneficial intention establishes beneficial consequence
that scale alone makes change systemic
open_checks: compare systems-change schools by ontology, power and intervention logic
build cases of failed and counterproductive systems change
profile.editorial_note: A developed working distinction for this release. The term remains contested and should be tested against rival usage and practice.

profile.title: Systems convening
profile.canonical_definition: Social-learning leadership that creates and sustains learning across boundaries in a social landscape. It need not derive from systems theory and is not a general synonym for partnership working, facilitation or institutional coordination.
profile.summary: Systems convening is social-learning leadership across boundaries. Conveners create new conversations and learning partnerships across a landscape, working with legitimacy, identity, agency, power and value creation.
profile.why_it_matters: It names work that is often real but invisible. It also needs protection from becoming a loose synonym for any cross-organisational meeting, network or partnership role.
key_distinctions: learning capability across a landscape vs competence inside one group
creating conditions for learning vs directing an agreed programme
systems convening vs systems theory or a systems methodology
practice_connections: work with boundaries, identity, agency and power
articulate value without claiming to control the result
common_misreadings: that it is any form of facilitation or partnership working
that it requires training in systems theory
that convening is politically neutral
that bringing everyone together guarantees agreement
open_checks: map cases where systems convening failed or lost legitimacy
compare systems convening with network weaving, brokerage and collective-impact roles
profile.editorial_note: A developed working distinction for this release. The term remains contested and should be tested against rival usage and practice.

profile.title: Systems laws
profile.canonical_definition: Systems laws and principles are recurrent statements about patterns, constraints and dynamics in systems. They support disciplined inquiry but do not operate as context-free prescriptions or deterministic predictions.
profile.summary: Systems laws and principles name recurrent constraints and dynamics that can sharpen inquiry. Their practical value depends on wording, boundary, context and the question being asked.
profile.why_it_matters: The atlas already had 33 public law entries, but the containing domain was hidden as metadata. Making it public helps readers distinguish a law corpus from a book, a method and a practitioner.
key_distinctions: law or principle vs deterministic equation
named regularity vs evidence in a case
common_misreadings: a named law proves a conclusion
all systems laws have the same status
context can be ignored
open_checks: record provenance and rival formulations for all 33 entries
distinguish scientific law, theorem, heuristic and practitioner principle
profile.editorial_note: Developed from cited public sources. The entry remains open to correction, rival accounts and stronger evidence.

profile.title: Systems leadership
profile.canonical_definition: An overloaded family of approaches ranging from leading an institutional 'system' more effectively, through creating more legitimate authority, to helping people develop new ways of organising. The phrase does not by itself specify the system, the leadership relation or whose purposes count.
profile.summary: Systems leadership is not one approach. It can mean better leadership of a set of institutions, better systems thinking by leaders, more legitimate shared authority, facilitation of system development, or support for new possibilities. These aims can conflict.
profile.why_it_matters: The label often creates false agreement. People may support 'systems leadership' while imagining very different distributions of authority, legitimacy, accountability and control.
key_distinctions: leadership of an institutional system vs leadership informed by systems thinking
improving system effectiveness vs challenging the legitimacy of existing power
leading change vs helping a system explore and develop itself
formal authority vs influence without authority
historical_lineage: collective, adaptive and facilitative leadership traditions

entry.label: Systems practice
entry.description: The situated use of systems ideas, methods and judgement to inquire and act in a problematic situation. It includes choosing boundaries, combining approaches, learning from consequences and allowing the inquiry to change the practitioner as well as the situation.

profile.title: Systems practice
profile.canonical_definition: The situated use of systems ideas, methods and judgement to inquire and act in a problematic situation. It includes choosing boundaries, combining approaches, learning from consequences and allowing the inquiry to change the practitioner as well as the situation.
profile.summary: Situated inquiry and action using systems concepts, approaches, models and intervention judgement. Professional practice includes choosing and combining approaches, working with stakeholders and power, testing consequences, learning and reflecting on the practitioner’s own participation.
profile.why_it_matters: Systems practice is wider than systems mapping and wider than any single methodology. The occupational standard and SCiO competence structure join systems concepts, multiple approaches, modelling, intervention, engagement and reflexive professional practice.
practice_connections: work with at least several approaches and know their limits
choose scope, scale and participation explicitly
learn from the consequences of intervention
common_misreadings: that systems practice is simply systems mapping
that the practitioner can remain outside the situation
that more tools create better judgement
that professionalisation removes contest and uncertainty
open_checks: connect capability statements to documented cases and failure modes
compare professional standards with practitioner-defined accounts of good work

entry.label: Systems theory
entry.description: A family of explanatory traditions concerned with systems, wholes, relations, organisation, feedback, boundaries, emergence and related phenomena. It is not one unified theory and does not automatically supply a method for intervention.

profile.title: Systems theory
profile.canonical_definition: A family of explanatory traditions concerned with systems, wholes, relations, organisation, feedback, boundaries, emergence and related phenomena. It is not one unified theory and does not automatically supply a method for intervention.
profile.summary: Systems theory is better read as a contested family of theories than as a single doctrine. Different traditions explain organisation, relation, boundary, feedback, emergence, hierarchy, viability or communication in materially different ways.
profile.why_it_matters: Practice becomes muddled when a broad theoretical vocabulary is treated as one agreed worldview, or when explanatory models are converted into prescriptions without showing the translation.
key_distinctions: one theory vs a family of traditions
formal, biological, social and organisational domains
first-order modelling vs reflexive and second-order accounts
practice_connections: say which theoretical tradition is being used
state the domain and limits of analogy
show the move from explanation to action
retain rival accounts where the field is not settled
common_misreadings: that all systems theories are compatible
that theory automatically provides a method
that using system language removes observer dependence
that a formal model supplies its own purpose and ethics
open_checks: develop a comparative history of major systems-theory traditions
map incompatible uses of system, organisation, information and complexity
profile.editorial_note: A developed working distinction for this release. The term remains contested and should be tested against rival usage and practice.

profile.canonical_definition: Relational and network-building work that notices, connects and strengthens people, groups and resources so new collaboration and self-organisation become possible. It overlaps with systems convening but usually puts more emphasis on network health and connection.
profile.summary: Systems weaving is used here for practical work which strengthens relationships, closes useful triangles, connects resources and helps networks become more capable of self-organisation and coordinated action.

connection and brokerage vs formal coordination
weaving vs convening a specific learning space
enabling self-organisation vs centrally directing a network

watch who remains excluded from the network
common_misreadings: that more connections are always better
that a visible network has no power centre
that weaving is a substitute for purpose or accountability
that systems weaving has one settled definition
open_checks: clarify how practitioners distinguish systems weaving from network weaving
add evidence on network overload, exclusion and brokerage power

profile.title: The Grammar of Systems II
profile.canonical_definition: Patrick Hoverstadt's guide to nine systems-thinking patterns and 33 systems laws and principles, intended to make the foundations of systems thinking usable in inquiry, design, strategy and transformation.
profile.summary: The Grammar of Systems II presents nine patterns of systems thinking and 33 laws and principles as a practical foundation for reasoning about order, change, complexity and uncertainty.
profile.why_it_matters: The 33 laws are useful only if they can be inspected as connected propositions rather than collected as slogans. This release makes the book-to-law structure explicit and adds a provisional, challengeable crosswalk from every law into concepts, other principles and practices already maintained in the atlas.
key_distinctions: thinking pattern vs law or principle
practice_connections: concept-to-practice navigation through the public graph
common_misreadings: the 33 items are universal equations
naming a law supplies a diagnosis
one book exhausts systems thinking
open_checks: add page-level locators for every law-to-concept connection
compare the first and second editions
record criticism and alternative formulations
review each provisional crosswalk with Grammar practitioners and domain stewards
profile.editorial_note: The 33 source-membership statements are source-backed. The added semantic crosswalk is deliberately provisional: it exposes an interpretation for review rather than asserting historical influence or formal equivalence.

entry.label: Transduction
entry.description: Transduction explains why a citizen's life becomes a case, a need becomes a code, work becomes a metric and strategy becomes a local instruction. The message is changed by the receiving world's categories and capacities.
entry.canonical_definition: A boundary process that transforms signals, meanings or varieties from one domain into a form another domain can register and act upon; it is never assumed to be lossless.

profile.title: Transduction
profile.canonical_definition: A boundary process that transforms signals, meanings or varieties from one domain into a form another domain can register and act upon; it is never assumed to be lossless.
profile.summary: Transduction explains why a citizen's life becomes a case, a need becomes a code, work becomes a metric and strategy becomes a local instruction. The message is changed by the receiving world's categories and capacities. Beer distinguishes a channel's capacity from the transducer's capacity at a boundary. His third principle requires the latter to match at least the former.
profile.why_it_matters: Transformation often fails at boundaries rather than within units. Seeing transduction reveals where meaning is lost, invented, protected or made actionable. Translation can discard a distinction that the communication channel could carry.
practice_connections: compare the sending and receiving codes
ask what is lost and newly created
design two-way transduction rather than one-way reporting
Compare the distinctions arriving at a boundary with those available after translation.
common_misreadings: transduction is just translation
loss is always failure
a common dashboard removes interpretation
the same information exists on both sides
A wider communication channel repairs every translation failure.
open_checks: Beer primary references
biological transduction
technical versus semantic uses
worked public-service cases
Specify the relevant variety before applying this organisational principle elsewhere.

entry.label: Variety
entry.description: The number of distinguishable possibilities in a specified set. Variety depends on which distinctions are available to an observer for a purpose; it is not a synonym for vague complexity.
entry.canonical_definition: The number of distinguishable elements or possible states in a specified set, sometimes expressed logarithmically; the distinctions and observer must be stated.

profile.title: Variety
profile.canonical_definition: The number of distinguishable elements or possible states in a specified set, sometimes expressed logarithmically; the distinctions and observer must be stated.
profile.summary: Variety counts distinguishable possibilities. A system may have many physical states but little usable variety if the observer cannot distinguish them or the regulator cannot select among effective responses.
profile.why_it_matters: Variety turns vague talk about complexity into a question about differences that matter for regulation. It also makes the observer visible: what counts as a different state depends on purpose, sensing and classification.
key_distinctions: variety vs diversity as a value
historical_lineage: Ashby developed variety as a central cybernetic measure
information theory provided related logarithmic tools
management cybernetics applied attenuation and amplification of variety
practice_connections: separate the variety seen by citizens, frontline workers and management
ask which options can actually change outcomes
do not add reporting variety that no one can absorb
common_misreadings: variety is objective and observer-free
more variety is always better
variety means diversity or complexity in general
every available option is usable
open_checks: formal relation to Shannon entropy
later variety engineering methods
profile.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.

entry.label: Variety attenuation
entry.description: Attenuation protects a regulator from being overwhelmed. It can simplify, buffer, aggregate or redesign demand. It can also erase inconvenient people and conditions if the boundary and purpose are wrong.
entry.canonical_definition: A deliberate reduction in effective variety so that relevant disturbances, signals or choices become tractable without pretending the discarded variety never existed.

profile.title: Variety attenuation

profile.summary: Attenuation protects a regulator from being overwhelmed. It can simplify, buffer, aggregate or redesign demand. It can also erase inconvenient people and conditions if the boundary and purpose are wrong.

entry.label: Viability
entry.description: Viability is not short-term survival or financial solvency. It concerns whether a system can keep producing itself as a coherent actor while its environment and internal conditions change.
entry.canonical_definition: The capacity of a system to continue as a recognisable whole by balancing present operations, regulation, learning, adaptation and identity under changing conditions.

profile.title: Viability
profile.canonical_definition: The capacity of a system to continue as a recognisable whole by balancing present operations, regulation, learning, adaptation and identity under changing conditions.
profile.summary: Viability is not short-term survival or financial solvency. It concerns whether a system can keep producing itself as a coherent actor while its environment and internal conditions change.
profile.why_it_matters: A viable organisation must handle today's work, disturbances and accountability while sensing and preparing for tomorrow. Central control cannot substitute for local regulatory capacity.
practice_connections: protect local autonomy while maintaining cohesion
separate current operations from future intelligence
test whether identity can change intelligently

viability means survival of the fittest
viability means never failing
a VSM diagram proves viability
central command creates cohesion

profile.editorial_note: Developed from public management-cybernetics, systems-practice and evolutionary-theory sources. Distinct theoretical traditions are not collapsed into one consensus account.

entry.label: Viable System Model (VSM)
entry.description: The Viable System Model is a management-cybernetic model for examining the functions and communications through which an organisation maintains autonomy, coordination, intelligence, identity and adaptation across recursive levels.
entry.canonical_definition: A management-cybernetic model for diagnosing and designing the functions and communications by which an organisation maintains viable autonomy and cohesion in a changing environment across recursive levels.

profile.title: Viable System Model
profile.canonical_definition: A management-cybernetic model for diagnosing and designing the functions and communications by which an organisation maintains viable autonomy and cohesion in a changing environment across recursive levels.
profile.summary: The VSM is a model of the functions and communications needed for an organisation to remain viable in a changing environment. It distinguishes autonomous operations from meta-systemic functions for coordination, internal regulation, intelligence and policy, and applies recursively.
profile.why_it_matters: The model makes the autonomy-cohesion problem explicit. It asks whether local operations can absorb relevant variety, whether conflicts are damped, whether the whole gains synergy, whether intelligence reaches strategy and whether identity closes the system without suffocating it.
historical_lineage: Beer developed the model from management practice and cybernetics
Brain of the Firm and Heart of Enterprise developed the theory
Diagnosing the System for Organizations provided a diagnostic guide
Cybersyn and later organisational practice extended its application
dependent_subsequents: Team Syntegrity as a related Beer practice
practice_connections: start from primary operations and their environments
map actual regulatory work rather than formal boxes
look for missing or overloaded functions
test communication channels for timeliness and capacity
common_misreadings: five boxes to assign to departments
a universal ideal structure
central control dressed as systems thinking
recursion is just more hierarchy
System 5 is the chief executive
governance is from outside the system
open_checks: primary page locators for recursion and requisite variety
critical and empirical evaluations
relations to power, ethics and democratic governance
profile.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.

entry.label: What the boundary cannot carry alone
entry.description: A relational encounter can improve while the organisation behind it remains unchanged. Taylor and Boxer distinguish form of response, scope of holding, health and fit, then propose four organisational conditions for sustaining relational public services.

profile.canonical_definition: A relational encounter can improve while the organisation behind it remains unchanged. Taylor and Boxer distinguish form of response, scope of holding, health and fit, then propose four organisational conditions for sustaining relational public services.
profile.why_it_matters: It makes the organisational demands behind relational practice explicit, including what evidence must be able to change.
key_distinctions: Form of response differs from scope of holding.
A wider scope is not necessarily healthier or better fitted to demand.
Relational behaviour differs from authority to revise rules and resources.
practice_connections: Start with actual demand in citizens’ words.
Ask who carries the work and risk, and what happens to learning.
open_checks: The authors describe a practitioner proposition, not a validated instrument.
Title-page v3 is retained; the source’s running footer still says v1.
